discovery: The jamming transition: a unified theory of rigidity in disordered matter
motivation: Why do sand, foams, emulsions, colloids and glasses become rigid? Liu and Nagel proposed that these disparate systems share one jamming phase diagram, governed by density, stress and temperature. With O'Hern, they found that jamming at zero temperature is a genuine critical point (Point J). Isostaticity sets it, and power-law scaling of pressure, shear modulus and excess contacts follows from it. Their theory predicted an excess of soft vibrational modes and a diverging length scale, both since confirmed in experiments on granular packings, colloids and foams. The framework now underpins our understanding of shear thickening in dense suspensions, of plasticity in amorphous solids, of tissue and cell-packing mechanics, and of how disordered mechanical metamaterials are designed. The work shows how simple ingredients produce universal emergent mechanics in everyday materials. It created a field that has shaped a generation of experiments and theory.
